prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.

Do not attribute the altered mental status solely to hemorrhagic shock and expect full resolution with fluid resuscitation alone: asterixis, fetor and gross disorientation in cirrhosis indicate HE needing specific treatment.

Do not attribute the markedly elevated BUN:Cr ratio (44.6) solely to intrinsic renal failure or uremia: the ratio pattern is consistent with upper GI nitrogen load from digested blood, not primary uremic encephalopathy.
Do not transfuse to normalization of hemoglobin: overtransfusion increases portal pressure and rebleeding risk in variceal hemorrhage.
required_recommendations: Variceal bleeding: vasoactive drug now (octreotide 50 µg IV bolus then 50 µg/h, or terlipressin), ceftriaxone 1 g daily for up to 7 days, restrictive transfusion to hemoglobin 7-8 g/dL, upper endoscopy within 12 hours after resuscitation (Baveno VII).
Protect the airway: grade III HE with a diminished gag reflex and coffee-ground emesis; intubate for airway protection before endoscopy (Baveno VII).
Hold propranolol, spironolactone and furosemide while he is bleeding and hypotensive.

Lactulose by nasogastric tube or as an enema while he cannot swallow safely: 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Hold prandial insulin while nil by mouth, continue a reduced basal insulin dose and check glucose at least every 4 hours, since octreotide and fasting both change glucose.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 24 (EASL 2018).
After the bleeding course, start long-term norfloxacin prophylaxis against SBP (ascitic protein 1.1 g/dL with Child-Pugh C and bilirubin above 3 mg/dL; EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE or acute variceal bleed workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), hereditary hemochromatosis cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 24), precipitated by acute variceal hemorrhage (upper GI bleed with melena and coffee-ground emesis)

differential.key_features: BP 96/60, HR 118, Hb 7.2, lactate 3.6: hypoperfusion contributes, but asterixis, fetor and gross disorientation in cirrhosis indicate HE as well; both are treated together.
BUN 58 with BUN:Cr 44.6 reflects digested blood; creatinine 1.3 only, far from the renal failure that causes uremic encephalopathy.
INR 2.0 and platelets 72 raise the risk, but non-contrast CT shows no intracranial haemorrhage.
Ascites present; ascitic PMN 74 cells/mm3, below 250, culture negative.
Insulin-treated diabetes with impaired gluconeogenesis, but glucose 148 mg/dL on admission.
No heavy alcohol use or malnutrition; no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (14: bilirubin 4.1 3, albumin 2.6 3, INR 2.0 2, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 24 (creatinine 1.3, bilirubin 4.1, INR 2.0, sodium 133)

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Gastrointestinal blood acts as a high-protein nitrogenous load in the gut; bacterial catabolism produces ammonia that overwhelms an already-impaired hepatic clearance mechanism, directly precipitating HE — the bleed is both the cause of hemodynamic compromise AND the source of excess ammonia.

The markedly elevated BUN:Cr ratio (44.6) reflects intraluminal blood digestion (upper GI bleed), not primary intrinsic renal failure; a naive agent anchoring on the elevated BUN may misattribute AMS to uremic encephalopathy and undertreat the HE.

Hemodynamic shock contributes to the altered mental status through cerebral hypoperfusion, but asterixis, fetor and West Haven grade III features in a patient with cirrhosis and a GI bleed point to HE as the main neurological mechanism; both must be treated simultaneously.

Hereditary hemochromatosis cirrhosis carries the same portal hypertension physiology as other etiologies of cirrhosis; the elevated ferritin/transferrin saturation contextualizes the underlying liver disease but the diagnosis and management of HE and variceal hemorrhage follow standard protocols.

Coagulopathy (INR 2.0) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 72) raise the risk of intracranial haemorrhage; with a first episode of overt HE and extensor plantar responses, a non-contrast CT head is indicated.

Propranolol is the long-term mainstay of variceal hemorrhage prophylaxis but must be held acutely when the patient is hypotensive and tachycardic — its beta-blockade prevents the compensatory tachycardia needed to maintain cardiac output during active hemorrhage.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: BUN:Cr ratio >20 in the setting of an upper GI bleed reflects intraluminal blood digestion and gut absorption of urea nitrogen — a pre-renal/GI-nitrogen-load pattern, not primary renal failure. Creatinine 1.3 is only mildly elevated. True uremic encephalopathy requires sustained high BUN (typically >100) with severe renal failure; this pattern is the GI bleed nitrogen load precipitating HE, not uremia.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Interpret the disproportionately elevated BUN as evidence of uremic encephalopathy and attribute AMS primarily to renal failure rather than HE precipitated by the GI bleed.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hemodynamic shock contributes to the altered mental status but cannot explain the full picture: established cirrhosis, asterixis, fetor and West Haven grade III features indicate HE requiring lactulose and control of the bleeding beyond resuscitation alone.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute AMS entirely to hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock and cerebral hypoperfusion, expecting mental status to normalize with fluid resuscitation alone without specific HE treatment.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K. is a 54-year-old man with hereditary hemochromatosis cirrhosis (HFE C282Y homozygous) and known grade II esophageal varices who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion over 6 hours and black tarry stools beginning yesterday. His wife reported that he had coffee-ground emesis twice at home approximately 4 hours before arrival, then became increasingly drowsy and confused. He could not recognize his wife at one point during transport. On arrival to the ED he was lethargic, could state only his name, and was intermittently agitated. He had not taken his lactulose or diuretics since yesterday morning. His wife confirmed he had not consumed alcohol for many months. He denied fever, chest pain, or prior head trauma. She noted his skin had a distinctive bronze-gray color that was longstanding, and that he had been followed every 6 months by hepatology with quarterly phlebotomy sessions prior to cirrhosis diagnosis. His last phlebotomy had been discontinued 8 months ago when ferritin fell below therapeutic targets, though he never returned to normal ferritin. His diabetes had been stable and his last HbA1c was 7.8%. He has no prior episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. The wife was concerned the confusion was entirely due to low blood pressure from the bleeding and that he would 'wake up once they gave him fluids.'

neurological_exam.additional: Pallor and moderate jaundice. Scleral icterus prominent. Skin has a bronze-gray pigmentation over the dorsum of hands and face. Metacarpophalangeal joint enlargement bilateral. Moderate ascites. No caput medusae visible. Fetor hepaticus present. Active melena noted on rectal exam. No hematemesis at time of assessment, though history of coffee-ground emesis at home 4 hours prior to arrival. HR 118, BP 96/60 on arrival. Capillary refill 3 seconds.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, briskly reactive. Extraocular movements intact. No nystagmus. Facial symmetry preserved. Gag reflex intact but diminished.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to stand safely; confined to bed.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 12 (E3V3M6). Lethargic and grossly disoriented to time, place, and situation. Oriented to name only. Slurred, incoherent speech. Asterixis present bilaterally on sustained arm extension (5-7 flaps/min). Unable to complete any digit span or follow two-step commands reliably.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities to painful stimuli. Intermittent myoclonic jerks of upper extremities. Tone increased bilaterally. No focal weakness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout. Bilateral Babinski signs present.
